questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The geometry that closes a dome
questions.learningObjective: Explain the geometric problem a dome creates over a square bay
questions.stem: During your survey of a ruined domed hall, the team notes that the four corners of the square bay are closed by curved surfaces that rise to meet a circle. What problem does this geometry solve?

options.text: It converts the square bay into a circular base so the dome can spring
It prevents rainwater from collecting in the corners of the bay
options.misconception: explains the corners as a drainage measure

options.text: It strengthens the corner piers against the weight of the dome
options.misconception: confuses the transition with a structural brace

options.text: It marks the corners that were rebuilt in a later campaign
options.misconception: reads the transition as a repair seam

questions.explanation: A dome is circular at its base but the room below is square, so the corners must be closed before the circle can begin. The transition surfaces complete that circle and give the dome its seat.
questions.hint: Compare the shape of the bay with the shape at the base.

questions.topic: The hoop push at the foot of a dome
questions.learningObjective: Compute the hoop thrust at the base of a dome
questions.stem: Your survey brief records a dome whose base circle is 12.0 metres across, with an estimated vertical load of 240 kN and a hoop thrust of 0.15 times that load. What hoop thrust in kN acts around the base circle?
questions.explanation: The hoop thrust is 0.15 x 240 kN = 36 kN, and it acts horizontally around the whole base circle rather than downward. A thin shell of that shape is easily crushed without support.
questions.hint: Multiply the thrust ratio by the vertical load.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a drum under a dome buys
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a drum under a dome provides

stimulus.body: The field note records a domed bay rising from a low cylindrical wall of masonry rings, and above that wall a set of arched openings that let the space between the wall and the shell pass through. The rings below are plain ashlar and clearly older than the arches above.

questions.stem: What does the presence of the plain ring below the arched openings buy the dome?

options.text: A place for the dome's weight to bear directly on the ground below
options.misconception: believes the drum carries the shell to the ground

options.text: Height to raise the shell clear of the piers, plus a place to absorb the hoop thrust
A second storey in which the survey team can store equipment
options.misconception: reads the drum as usable storage space

options.text: A wall to block the wind from the plain before it reaches the shell
options.misconception: assigns the drum a purely climatic role

questions.explanation: The drum lifts the shell above the level of the arcade, so the dome can be seen whole, and its ring of arches gives the hoop thrust a place to be taken. The flat drum ring does not do that work.
questions.hint: Think about height gained and thrust absorbed.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A drum described as a ring of piers
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a ring of piers gains height rather than mass
questions.stem: Write a short note explaining why a dome raised on a ring of piers is described as gaining height rather than gaining mass.

answer.exemplar: A ring of piers carries the shell above the level of the arcade, so the dome appears as a separate, elevated object that can be seen from the ground rather than pressed down among the supports. Because the shell is not let down to the piers, the weight of the dome is spread across many points instead of being concentrated on the wall below, which is what frees the walls to carry their arches and openings.

questions.explanation: The piers substitute a framework of supports for a continuous wall, and that framework raises the shell. Height and mass are different gains: one lifts the dome, the other loads the wall.
questions.hint: Say what the piers do to the shell's position.

questions.stem: Your survey log gives the internal height of a bell tower as 42.0 metres and the height of the belfry chamber within it as 12.0 metres. How many metres of the tower lie below the belfry chamber?

questions.topic: The circulation of a cloister
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the covered walk of a cloister organises
questions.stem: In your survey of a monastic precinct, you record a covered walk running around a square central space, entered from a corner. What does that circulation organise?

options.text: A processional route that ends at the centre of the open court
options.misconception: assumes the route terminates in the court

options.text: A direct shortcut from the gate to the far corner of the court
options.misconception: reads the walk as a shortcut across the court

options.text: A continuous route that returns to its start without ever entering the court
A service path that deliberately avoids the covered walk altogether
options.misconception: assumes the walk is not used for circulation

questions.explanation: A cloister walk is a ring, and the ring is the point: the walker can circulate, meet, and return without ever crossing the open space it encloses. The court is held apart and stays quiet.

questions.stem: A survey of a cloister garth records a square court of 28.0 metres on each side, with a covered walk 4.0 metres deep running around it. What is the total width across the court plus both walks in metres?

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The circulation of a cloister
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a cloister walk is read as a device for circulation
questions.stem: Explain to the survey team why the covered walk of a cloister is read as a device for circulation rather than as a set of rooms.

answer.exemplar: The walk is described as a ring, and a ring cannot be entered and left in the middle: a person who steps onto it is committed to walking until the loop returns him to the point of entry. That single rule produces the cloister's characteristic traffic, with processions, meetings and daily errands all moving around the court and never across it, which is what keeps the open space quiet and separate from the busy outer precinct.

questions.explanation: A ring plan forces movement into a continuous circuit, and a circuit can be used without any room being defined. The cloister is organised by the route itself.
questions.hint: Say what the shape of the route forces a walker to do.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The geometry that closes a dome
questions.learningObjective: Identify the transition device that closes a described square bay

stimulus.body: The field note describes a square room of 14.0 metres, in the middle of which a round dome springs from a circle. The four corners of the room are not open; each is filled by a curved surface of masonry that slopes down to the corner.

questions.stem: Given the note, which device closes the corners of the surveyed square room?

options.text: Flying buttresses, which carry the corner load from outside the room
options.misconception: confuses an external support with an internal transition

options.text: Squinches, which are small arches built across each corner
options.misconception: names the arch device instead of the curved triangle

options.text: A squashed barrel, which flattens the circle into the square
options.misconception: invents a squashed barrel transition

options.text: Pendentives, which are curved triangles rising from each corner

questions.explanation: A smooth curved surface sloping from the corner up to the circle is a pendentive, while a squinch would be an arch standing across the corner. The note describes the surface, not an arch.
questions.hint: Ask whether the corner is closed by a surface or an arch.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The open court inside a cloister
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a cloister court is described as a room without a roof
questions.stem: Explain to the survey team why the open court at the centre of a cloister is described as a room without a roof.

answer.exemplar: A roofed room is defined by walls and a ceiling, and the cloister court is defined by walls but no ceiling at all. Its enclosure comes entirely from the surrounding walk, which frames four sides of sky and admits light and rain from above. Reading the court as a room explains why the open square is so carefully proportioned and why planting or a well sits at its centre, and why the walk is turned inward rather than outward.

questions.explanation: The court has boundaries but no cover, so it is enclosed in plan only. Everything about its character follows from being a room open to the sky.
questions.hint: Say what the court has and lacks compared to a room.

questions.topic: A drum described as a ring of piers
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a ring of separate piers carries a dome

stimulus.body: The field note records the base of a dome standing on a circle of separate stone piers rather than on a continuous wall. questions.stem: What does the note's ring of separate piers tell you about how the drum works?

options.text: The open ring lets the wind turn the shell, which is why the dome sways
options.misconception: invents a wind-driven sway

options.text: The ring of piers is a screen hiding the back of the nave from the choir

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A described belfry opening
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a belfry opening is a shaped aperture
questions.stem: Explain to the survey team why a belfry opening is described as a shaped aperture rather than a plain hole in the wall.

answer.exemplar: A plain opening in a thick wall is weak and, more importantly, muffled, because the depth of the wall above it blocks the sound. A belfry opening is shaped and splayed so that the aperture is narrow at the outer face and wide at the inner, which directs the sound outward in a beam and removes the resonant flat surface that would swallow it. The opening is thus an instrument, not a gap in the masonry.

questions.explanation: The shape controls where the sound goes and how much the wall impedes it. A well-formed aperture is tuned to the room it faces.
questions.hint: Say what the shape of the aperture does to the sound.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The vertical function of a bell tower
questions.learningObjective: Explain why bell tower height is a function rather than a display
questions.stem: Explain to the survey team why the height of a bell tower is described as a function rather than as a matter of display.

answer.exemplar: The tower's height is the mechanism, not the monument. Raised bells convert a limited swing into a swinging arc at a distance, and the height of the arc determines the reach of the call, so a settlement can be heard from far beyond its own walls. Height also lifts the sound clear of roofs and of the wind turbulence near the ground, which is why the belfry is placed at the top and the shaft below is treated as carrying weight rather than making noise.

questions.explanation: Height determines how far a call carries and how clear of obstructions it is. The lower shaft exists to carry the belfry up to that useful height.
questions.hint: Say what height does for the reach of the call.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The geometry that closes a dome
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a square chamber can be covered by a round dome
questions.stem: Write a short survey note explaining why a square chamber can be covered by a round dome, and what has to happen at the corners.

answer.exemplar: The shell of a dome is a surface of revolution, so it can only begin from a circle, and a square chamber has no circle to offer: its four corners sit outside any circle that touches its sides. Something must therefore fill the space between the square and that circle, and the traditional devices are the squinch, an arch built across the corner, and the pendentive, a curved triangle of masonry that thins as it rises. Both restore the circle and hand the shell a continuous seat.

questions.explanation: A dome's base is a circle and a room's plan is a square, so the corners must be filled. Squinches and pendentives are the two ways of restoring the circle.
questions.hint: Say what a dome's base needs and what fills the gap.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A drum described as a ring of piers
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate what a ring of piers gains and gives up against a wall
questions.stem: Explain to the survey team what a dome supported on a ring of piers gains and what it gives up, compared with a dome on a continuous wall.

answer.exemplar: A ring of piers gains height and light, because the shell can be lifted clear of the arcade and the gaps between the supports keep the base open, so the dome reads as a separate object above the building. It gives up the continuous wall's ability to absorb the hoop thrust in mass, so the shell's push must be carried by the piers and by a hoop of reinforcement tying them together, and the composition becomes structurally explicit rather than massive.

questions.explanation: The open frame buys height and openness at the price of the mass that a solid wall provides. The thrust has to be handled by the piers and a binding hoop.
questions.hint: Compare what the open frame gains with what it costs.

answer.exemplar: Raising the shell on a drum gives the building three things at once. The dome stands clear of the arcade, so a visitor standing in the nave can see it whole rather than looking up into it, and its profile is legible from outside. questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The hoop push at the foot of a dome
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the hoop thrust of a dome spreads around its base
questions.stem: Explain to the survey team what the hoop thrust at the foot of a dome is, and why it spreads rather than concentrating.

answer.exemplar: The hoop thrust is the outward push that the shell of a dome develops around its base, and it runs in every direction at once, like the pressure in a hoop. Because a dome carries its load along meridians that meet the base all the way round, the force is not gathered at four points as in a crossing vault but distributed continuously around the whole circle, which is why the base needs a continuous ring of support rather than four heavy piers.

questions.explanation: The push acts horizontally in every direction around the base circle. A continuous ring of support is needed because the load arrives all the way round.
questions.hint: Say how many directions the push acts in.
